Each diagram in the model has a Documentation box (also referred to as Diagram Info). The bold text at the top of each diagram states the purpose of the diagram. The remaining text provides additional information about the content of the diagram and how to interpret it.

 

The text may also include hyperlinks (blue text) to provide dynamic cross-references to related diagrams and elements within the model, or external references on the Internet.

 

This diagram is organized into numbered sections to provide an overview of the model. The numbers in each section indicate a suggested reading order to cover all the diagrams. This is intended to provide a starting point, but it is not a strict order - the reader is encouraged to explore the model independently to gain a deeper understanding.

ownedComment.body:
The MVF metamodel as per the natural language (PDF) beta specification at www.omg.org/spec/MVF/1.0/Beta1/PDF

The MVF metamodel presented on this diagram is the main diagram for the MVF metamodel. It is based on the XMI-based metamodel and adds information that is in the RDF and PDF versions but missing from the XMI. For the MboeMappingRelation extension to the metamodel, see diagram MVF Metamodel - MboeMappingRelation replaces Generalization.

 

It is assumed that the different versions of the specification have the following precedence.

1      XMI (used as the basis for the PDF-based UML metamodel

The XMI broadly corresponds to the diagrams in the PDF, but some elements shown in the PDF do not appear in the XMI - some of the issues addressed here are documented at: issues.omg.org/issues/spec/MVF)

2      PDF (additional metamodel elements in the PDF version, such as MVFElement, are added to the XMI-based metamodel.

The PDF version is assumed to have highest precedence because this provides information about both the XMI and RDF versions.

3      RDF (all elements of the RDF-based metamodel retained "as imported" unless otherwise noted).

Because the purpose of this model is to provide a UML profile for MVF, it is logical to base it on the XMI (i.e. XMI) version of the metamodel.

  

The main reason for this precedence assumption is that it best preserves the XMI specification, which is the version intended to be used for modelling in UML. This model provides fixes for the problems encountered with XMI and PDF versions based on the RDF specification. In order to provide an RDF interface to UMlL models created with the MVF profile presented here, traceability links between UML classes/attributes to equivalent RDF elements/properties are provided.

 

The MVF PDF specification is not clear about the mapping between the associations shown on the metamodel and the equivalent object properties that implement relationships in OWL. However, it is clear from the RDF specification that all the relationships are derived directly from owl:topObjectProperty (the object property that relates every two individuals).

 

Because the MBOE metamodel extends MVF with SKOS relations that are not captured by the MVF metamodel, an additional assertion is shown to assert that the MVF Generalization relationship subsets the SKOS property is in semantic relation with. The equivalence of MVFEntry and skos:concept is also asserted per Section 4 of the PDF under the heading Model Element.

 

In the course of creating this metamodel (which combines information from all three versions, but is based on the XMI), it was found that the RDF version appeared to be more correct and complete. In future work it may be useful to align the UML profile with the RDF version directly and bypass the XMI. Given that this metamodel is based on the Beta specification, however, it would be better to submit the problems identified here as issues and wait for the full release (which will hopefully fix the several problems that are causing the current PDF/XMI/RDF misalignment).

 

Note that diagrams showing all the annotations in the RDF file are not included with this model (unlike for SKOS). This is because a full set of annotated diagrams for all the MVF ontologies is available in Section 9 of the MVF Specification PDF (note that these have not be checked for consistency with the RDF by this author).

The main MVF metamodel based on Multiple Vocabulary Facility (MVF) Ontology.

This the main MVF ontology, which is one of the ontologies loaded by the imported AboutMvf.rdf.

 

This differs from the metamodel based on the PDF specification, see MVF Metamodel - Per PDF (no missing elements), which in turn differs from the imported XMI version of the model, see MVF Metamodel - Per XMI (missing elements) and MVF Metamodel - Side by side (RDF vs PDF/XMI). Theoretically all versions should all agree. For the resolution stategy see: MVF Metamodel - Per PDF (no missing elements).

Definition of the tagged values for stereotypes used in the MVF profile with mappings to corresponding metamodel attributes

The types assigned to tagged value definitions on this diagram are UML primitives from CCM's standard UML profile, as used by the corresponding MVF XMI attribute, unless changes are indicated by a pale blue note. These primitives are used in preference to RDF based primitives (e.g. rdf:langString, cmns-txt:Text, which are based on xsd:String; see RDF 1.1 Recommendation, Section 5, Datatypes). This choice is also guided by the decision to take the MVF XMI as the primary basis for this metamodel and helps to ensure the portability of the UML profile when deployed in environments without access to this metamodel. When generating RDF based ontologies from UML models built with this profile, consideration should be give to the choice of primitive that these attributes are mapped to - the equivalent RDF properties are asserted indirectly via subsetting relations to attributes of classes in the MVF XMI metamodel, which in turn can be traced via further subsetting relations in the RDF metamodel. Note that there is not a one to one correspondence between the attributes of the MVF XMI and MVF RDF classes (see MVF Metamodel - RDF to XMI/PDF equivalent class mappings). If in doubt, default to typing RDF conversions with XSD datatypes, but note this may result in information loss.

 

The tagged value to attribute mappings are split across several diagrams to improve readability. See also MVF Base Profile - Tagged values mapped to metamodel attributes (not mvfElement, vocabularyEntry) and MVF Base Profile - Tagged values mapped to metamodel attributes (mvfElement)

An MVF Entry is a unit of knowledge created by a unique combination of characteristics, i.e., a concept. An MVF entry is contained in exactly one MVF dictionary and may be linked to by one or more model elements that represent that concept in the modeling environment. It will be linked to by vocabulary entries of alternative vocabularies that express the same concept in a different natural language or vernacular. It is possible that some concepts are not mapped to an entry in any vocabulary, and that not all MVF entries are associated with model elements in the active modeling environment. Though MVFEntries are not intended to provide a concept modeling capability, two specific associations are available to provide context, in the scneario of mapping a Model Element to an existing MVF Entry. It is the responsibility of conformant tools to make use of these to meet the needs of their users: • broader: this typically links fo a MVF Entry representing a more general element of the same typo (e.g. a superclass) • context: this typically references a containing MVF Entry such as that for a Package (for a MVF Entry representing a class) or a Class (for one representing a Property).

Attribute for an open ended reference or identifier related to the concept or thing represented by the MVFEntry. This could reference an external ontology element, concept specification, model, description, web page, or other resource.

Note that this attribute is labeled status in Section 8.7 of the PDF specification, termStatus in Section 9.1 of the PDF and mvfEntryStatus in the XMI. The equivalence of these attributes is assumed for this model.

The MVF Spec does not dictate what values should be adopted for entry status. The enumerated values here are based on the idea that a term goes through the following life-cycle (in order): DICTIONARY_DEF - a term is in use in a context but no formal definition of the corresponding concept has been proposed or adopted for the relevant context, relying on dictionary definitions PROPOSED - term and definition have been proposed but not approved DRAFT - a term and definition have been provisionally accepted, subject to an approval process PUBLISHED - term and definition are approved and published in an official document (note: considered as official in the context, may not be official in other contexts) WITHDRAWN - term no longer in use i.e. officially withdrawn This possibly duplicates isDeprecated in some contexts, but not necessarily - for example a concept from a standard may remain in use on a project after the standard is withdrawn because it was current when the product was developed.

When CCM transforms OWL ontologies as they are imported from RDF to UML, any RDF properties that the transformer doesn't recognize are rendered as UML associations. This works well for most relations (because a lot of relations in UML models tend to be associations), but it is problematic when the semantics of the property would be better represented with a standard UML relationship other than association. In this model, this applies in particular to relationships that indicate that one element depends on another (e.g. a definition adopted from another vocabulary), which are more naturally represented as UML dependencies. UML associations do not have an attribute that can be used to indicate either general directionality or dependency: the only support for directional attributes is for reading direction (which does not suffice as an assertion of dependency) and navigability (which is a dependency, but only applies to efficiency of runtime access).

 

There is no way for the importer to know the semantics of the imported property automatically (without connecting it to some kind of reasoning engine). This means that the semantics must be applied manually by human review of the model. There are several possible ways to resolve this.

  • Repurpose the navigability property to indicate a directional association
    • This is a fairly common informal practice adopted by many modelers in search of a way to add an arrowhead to an association, but has several drawbacks. The UML 2.5.1 specification states that "Navigability means that instances participating in links at runtime (instances of an Association) can be accessed efficiently from instances at the other ends of the Association". For conceptual modeling, this is not a particular useful property, so within controlled contexts (e.g. a model used only by a single organization) it can be acceptable to redefine the meaning of the navigability arrowhead, provided everyone working on the model is made aware. Because the intended output of this model is a broadly useful UML profile for modeling multiple contexts, this is not an appropriate choice here.
  • Manually refactor the type on the each imported relationship (e.g. change its type from association to dependency)
    • This could cause compatibility problems if the model is used to generate 'round trip' outputs to RDF because information is potentially lost (associations have a different set of attributes than dependencies).
  • Establish newly created "mirror" relationships with the correct type (e.g. dependency) in the metamodel, with traceability links to the property that was imported as an association.
    • This approach is time consuming, increases the maintenance burden, and generates unnecessary duplication.
  • Retain Association as the base type and extend this through inheritance of additional properties through multiple inheritance (e.g. those relationships that are dependencies would have stereotypes «association» and «dependency»).
    • This is a fairly clean solution, but it is not parsimonious because the relationships inherit additional properties that are not strictly necessary. This potentially undermines the benefits of the separation of concerns implicit in the intentional disjointedness of these metaclasses in the UML specification.
  • The cleanest, most parsimonious solution identified, which is used here, is to define custom stereotypes based on standard UML metaclasses in a profile based on the metamodel (see mappingRelation - Top levels).
    • Custom stereotypes ensure that the relationships only have the required properties from the relevant metaclasses. This avoids unnecessary multiple inheritance.

Adopting this final approach means that it is not possible to define relationships based on the custom stereotypes in the metamodel, because this would otherwise create a circular dependency by applying a stereotype in the model that is also defined by the same model. Avoiding this ensures a degree of self-bootstrapping, in that the model can be loaded without needing to preload any profiles to support custom types (except those used from the CCM profile) and can generate the MBOE profile from only standard UML metaclasses.

 

One side effect of the adopted approach is that it is not possible to represent the extensions to skos:mappingRelation directly in the UML metamodel, because CCM converts all the relevant RDF object properties to associations. ISO 3166 provides widely, though not universally, applicable coded representations of names of countries, dependencies, and other areas of particular geopolitical interest and their subdivisions. - ISO 3166-1 (Country codes) establishes codes that represent the current names of countries, dependencies, and other areas of particular geopolitical interest, on the basis of lists of country names obtained from the United Nations. - ISO 3166-2 (Country subdivision code) establishes a code that represents the names of the principal administrative divisions, or similar areas, of the countries, etc. included in the ISO 3166-1. - ISO 3166-3 (Code for formerly used names of countries) establishes a code that represents non-current country names, i.e., the country names deleted from ISO 3166 since its first publication in 1974.
The United Nations Standard Country or Area Codes for Statistical Use (M49), described at https://unstats.un.org/unsd/methodology/m49/, provides further regional classification for countries by continent, region within a continent, and sub-regions within regions that are widely used as well, and so this ontology is designed to support the M49 code set as well. M49 reuses the ISO 3166 codes for countries and some regions, and augments that with additional, broader regional codes.
This ontology provides a reference model to support the first two parts of ISO 3166, along with the other coding systems mentioned above.

The current version of the ontology (including subordinate modules containing the language names and codes) provides a unique English name (i.e., the reference name from 639-3) for each language, with UTF-8 encoded literals specifying alternates in English, French, and Indigenous languages where present in the standard, and in German corresponding to the names on the LoC web site.
1. Where multiple English names occur in 639-1 and 639-2, we have used the primary name specified in 639-2:1998 superseded by the latest revision posted by the registration authority, or, where multiples are specified by the registration authority, the reference name from ISO 639-3 as the 'named individual name' for a given language. For languages specified in ISO 639-1, there is at least one English name and at least one French name for every language, corresponding to exactly one alpha-2 code. Most languages from ISO 639-1 have at least one indigenous name. Most languages with codes available from the Library of Congress also have at least one German name. The correspondence between the alpha-2 codes and languages are made explicit in the individuals representing the codes themselves, and can be inferred for the languages using an OWL DL reasoner.
2. This release of the ontology covers all languages specified in parts 1 and 2 of the standard, and categorizes the alpha-3 codes from part 2 according to the categorization scheme provided in parts 3 and 4. Subsequent releases of the ontology will address additional languages covered in part 3, as well as additional components of the standard, such as equivalence to standards representing relevant scripts, as they become available, and the language groups covered by ISO 639-5.
3. We have used individuals to represent all alpha-2 and alpha-3 codes, which, in turn, have matching strings (tags) associated with them for use in a variety of applications to facilitate reasoning and mapping. The strings are provided as datatype properties of the individuals to support applications that may require them for RFC 4646-style tagging.
4. Note that some tools, including certain UML tools, are case insensitive. Thus, in cases where a language name collides with an alpha-2 or alpha-3 code, (i.e., Ga, Ewe, Fon, Ido, Lao, Tiv, Twi, Vai, and Yao), the names for the individual codes have been extended with '_1' (e.g., 'ewe_1').

These include: (1) Bihari is included in the 2002 version of 639-1, in the 1998 version of 639-2, and in the online codes posted by the Library of Congress in 2007 for parts 1 and 2, with part 1 code of 'bh' and part 2 bibliographic and terminology codes of 'bih'. Since then, the language element has been renamed 'Bihari languages', in both English and French, without change to the corresponding language codes. The latest version of the code sets reflect this modification. Our assumption is that the trigraph for Bihari is a collective language code, which is supported by online research in Eastern Indic languages. (2) Serbo-Croatian was included in the 2002 version of 639-1, with part 1 code 'sh'. It was not mentioned in the 1998 version of 693-2, but appears in 639-3 with a language identifier of 'hbs', without codes for 639-2. As of 2010, Serbo-Croation has been eliminated from ISO 639-1 and 639-2 codes altogether, and the ontology reflects this. An MVF Entry is a unit of knowledge created by a unique combination of characteristics, i.e., a concept. An MVF entryis contained in exactly one MVF dictionary and may be linked to by one or more model elements that represent that concept in the modeling environment. It will be linked to by vocabulary entries of alternative vocabularies that express the same concept in a different natural language or vernacular. It is possible that some concepts are not mapped to an entry in any vocabulary, and that not all MVF entries are associated with model elements in the active modeling environment. Though MVFEntries are not intended to provide a concept modeling capability, two specific associations are available to provide context, in the scneario of mapping a Model Element to an existing MVF Entry. It is the responsibility of conformant tools to make use of these to meet the needs of their users: • broader: this typically links fo a MVF Entry representing a more general element of the same typo (e.g. a superclass) • context: this typically references a containing MVF Entry such as that for a Package (for a MVF Entry representing a class) or a Class (for one representing a Property).

A Vocabulary is a set of representations of concepts (terms and definitions) for the language of a particular speech community that is expressed in a specified natural language. A speech community may create a vocabulary by importing a one or more existing vocabulary and overriding selected terms, adding terms for new concepts and (implicitly) incorporating the remaining terms and definitions of the existing vocabulary. This mechanism may be employed to introduce synonyms as the primary terms of the specializing community. Both vocabularies should be in the same natural language so that definitions remain meaningful.
Id as per ISO 639-1.

A community is a group of people that share a natural language and have a shared set of terms used to express concepts in their domain of interest. We refer to a set of terms that is distinguished from general use of the natural language as a vernacular. The community may be persons that share a profession, are members of the same enterprise or organization or are collaborating on a particular technology.

A workspace is an MVF element that references a consistent set of the MVF dictionaries and vocabularies to be used in a modeling environment. It’s the responsibility of a conformant modeling tool to select the current active Workspace, which is then used to resolve from a Model Element to the most appropriate Vocabulary Entry to provide the term and definition.

The MVF metamodel as per the natural language (PDF) beta specification at www.omg.org/spec/MVF/1.0/Beta1/PDF

The MVF metamodel presented on this diagram is the main diagram for the MVF metamodel. It is based on the XMI-based metamodel and adds information that is in the RDF and PDF versions but missing from the XMI. For the MboeMappingRelation extension to the metamodel, see diagram MVF Metamodel - MboeMappingRelation replaces Generalization.

 

It is assumed that the different versions of the specification have the following precedence.

1      XMI (used as the basis for the PDF-based UML metamodel

The XMI broadly corresponds to the diagrams in the PDF, but some elements shown in the PDF do not appear in the XMI - some of the issues addressed here are documented at: issues.omg.org/issues/spec/MVF)

2      PDF (additional metamodel elements in the PDF version, such as MVFElement, are added to the XMI-based metamodel.

The PDF version is assumed to have highest precedence because this provides information about both the XMI and RDF versions.

3      RDF (all elements of the RDF-based metamodel retained "as imported" unless otherwise noted).

Because the purpose of this model is to provide a UML profile for MVF, it is logical to base it on the XMI (i.e. XMI) version of the metamodel.

  

The main reason for this precedence assumption is that it best preserves the XMI specification, which is the version intended to be used for modelling in UML. This model provides fixes for the problems encountered with XMI and PDF versions based on the RDF specification. In order to provide an RDF interface to UMlL models created with the MVF profile presented here, traceability links between UML classes/attributes to equivalent RDF elements/properties are provided.

 

The MVF PDF specification is not clear about the mapping between the associations shown on the metamodel and the equivalent object properties that implement relationships in OWL. However, it is clear from the RDF specification that all the relationships are derived directly from owl:topObjectProperty (the object property that relates every two individuals).

 

Because the MBOE metamodel extends MVF with SKOS relations that are not captured by the MVF metamodel, an additional assertion is shown to assert that the MVF Generalization relationship subsets the SKOS property is in semantic relation with. The equivalence of MVFEntry and skos:concept is also asserted per Section 4 of the PDF under the heading Model Element.

 

In the course of creating this metamodel (which combines information from all three versions, but is based on the XMI), it was found that the RDF version appeared to be more correct and complete. In future work it may be useful to align the UML profile with the RDF version directly and bypass the XMI. Given that this metamodel is based on the Beta specification, however, it would be better to submit the problems identified here as issues and wait for the full release (which will hopefully fix the several problems that are causing the current PDF/XMI/RDF misalignment).

 

Note that diagrams showing all the annotations in the RDF file are not included with this model (unlike for SKOS). This is because a full set of annotated diagrams for all the MVF ontologies is available in Section 9 of the MVF Specification PDF (note that these have not be checked for consistency with the RDF by this author).

The documentation for MVFEntry defines the role MVFEntry::context as: "context: this typically references a containing MVF Entry such as that for a Package (for a MVF Entry representing a class) or a Class (for one representing a Property)." [duplicates: MVF PDF Specification Section 8.5]. It is therefore clear that context can be provided by containment, but the specification does not offer further explicit explanation for the way context is represented in MVF. The term context is, however, used loosely throughout, especially when discussing VocabularyEntry, for example: "A vocabulary entry associates a definition and term (name, designation, abbreviation) with one concept (MVF Entry) in the context of the vocabulary" [Section 8.7, see also Table 10.2] ". Table 10.2 also uses the term context when defining abbreviation: "a shortened designation for a term that is used synonymously with that term in the context of a given vocabulary or dictionary". This usage seems to suggest that a representation of context that encompasses other subtypes of MVFElement would be useful (even necessary).

 

Because there is an equivalent OWL ontology to the XMI version, it is assumed that the OWL (and more generally, semantic web) convention of open-world assumption shall apply to both OWL and UML versions of MVF. As such, the absence of a relationship from the model does not necessarily mean that it is an invalid relationship (it may be valid, but just not included in the model). Nonetheless, it is somewhat surprising that MVF only admits context elements that are typed with MVFEntry. The way EntryContext is defined implies that only instances of MVFEntry can be used to define a given context, and similarly that only MVFEntry can act in the role entryInContext. Based on the role names, only the latter is evidently valid, i.e. that only Things that are entries (MVFEntry) should be able to qualify as entryInContext. It is not evident, however, why other types of MVFElement are not able to act in the role of context. It may be useful to consider changing this relationship to allow all MVFElement to act in the context role (i.e. the association end MVFEntry::context would be disconnected from MVFEntry and reconnected to MVFElement to become association end MVFElement::context).

 

Consider also that MVFEntry is equivalent to skos::Concept (see MVF Metamodel - Assertions for joining MVF with SKOS extensions). It seems unnecessarily restrictive to admit only concepts as contexts (or context-forming). If this relationship were broadened further to be between Thing and entryInContext, it would allow other types in the MVF ontology to form contexts.

 

More broadly still, it seems worth considering that any Thing may be either a thingInContext or Context, or both. By representing this explicitly (which as stated above, it is not excluded by the MVF specification), it is possible to support more worldviews of context without losing the specificity of the entryInContext that is intended by MVF

 

It is not clear how the nature of the context provided to entryInContext should be captured (e.g. which of the six W questions - who, where, what, where, when, why and how - does it answer?). For this work such information will be captured in the documentation for the relationship when it is instantiated. In summary, it is understood that: the specified scope of MVFEntry::context is narrow (includes containment, but otherwise not unambiguously defined); MVF also considers a broader view of context that admits other types (at least: VocabularyEntry and abbreviation) that is not captured in the metamodel; a more general representation of context can be added to the model, which supports the existing usage of MVFEntry::context and formalises the existing looser usage of the term in a compatible manner.

The MVF Beta 1.0 PDF specification Section 4 makes clear that MVFEntry  is equivalent to Concept, as defined by ISO 1087:2019 "Terminology work and terminology science — Vocabulary", i.e.

 

a unit of knowledge created by a unique combination of characteristics

 

The equivalence is only asserted in natural language in the MVF Beta 1.0 PDF specification. In accordance with the PDF, Concept is represented in this model by the class MVFEntry, which is included in the imported MVF.xmi ontology. AboutMVF.rdf includes two ontologies based on ISO 1087:2019, but neither these nor the other machine readable MVF specifications (XMI and RDF formats) define an object for Concept. Instead, the term MVFEntry is defined in the Multiple Vocabulary Facility (MVF) Ontology and used throughout the suite of specifications in place of the term Concept, i.e.:

 

An MVF Entry is a unit of knowledge created by a unique combination of characteristics, i.e., a concept. ...

[for full definition see MVFEntry]

 

AboutMVF.rdf does however load the SKOS/core ontology, and therefore models built on the semantic web version of MVF also have access to the definition of skos:concept i.e.:

 

An idea or notion; a unit of thought.

[in this model Imported Ontologies::core::Concept ].

 

This relationship is not asserted when the resource ontologies are imported by CCM, but is essential for the developing an extension that combines both the MVF and SKOS metamodels.

 

Be aware also that there is an issue in the SKOS RDF specification with the range of sub-properties of 'skos:is in semantic relation with' being imported by CCM as from Concept to Thing rather than as reflexive Concept to Concept relationships. This is discussed in detail on diagram SKOS Metamodel - Per RDF classes and associations (no annotations).

The SKOS property skos:semanticRelation (on this diagram the association end 'is in semantic relation with') has several sub-properties, which include mapping relations. The sub-properties are rendered in UML as subsetted assoications between Concept and Thing, rather than as reflexive relationships from Concept to Concept (Concept to Thing is how they are transformed by the CCM OWL importer). The underlying reason for this disparity is understood to be that the SKOS core RDF specification does not declare the rdf:range and rdf:domain of the sub-properties, so the importer assumes the broadest possible domain and range, which is Thing. However, when range and domain are asserted for a parent class (here: Concept), this means that the range/domain constraint does in fact apply to all sub-properties of that parent class for which the domain/range is asserted. Per the SKOS core RDF specification:

 

The triple (P rdfs:range C) states that P is an instance of the class rdf:Property, that C is an instance of the class rdfs:Class and that the resources denoted by the objects of triples whose predicate is P are instances of the class C.)...

A triple of the form: (P rdfs:domain C) states that P is an instance of the class rdf:Property, that C is a instance of the class rdfs:Class and that the resources denoted by the subjects of triples whose predicate is P are instances of the class C.

 

The above considerations mean that for this model it is preferable to model the subsetted relations from Concept to Concept instead of, as shown here, from Concept to Thing. For further information on the application of this see diagram MVF Base Profile - Relationship stereotypes mapped to metamodel relationships.

The 'disjoint' constraint on the generalization set has been manually set to TRUE in CCM after import. When originally imported, this was set to FALSE (i.e. 'overlapping'), which contradicts the «Disjoint With» relation between Collection and Concept. The SKOS specification defines the 'core:member' property (i.e. 'has member' on this diagram) with two ranges: 'skos:Collection', 'skos:Concept'. According to the RDF 1.2 schema for rdfs:range: "Where P has more than one rdfs:range property, then the resources denoted by the objects of triples with predicate P are instances of all the classes stated by the rdfs:range properties." This implies that multiple RDF ranges are in a non-exclusive OR relationship, which the CCM OWL importer interprets as complete and overlapping constraints. Unfortunately, the importer does not detect that the separate disjointness constraint in the RDF file tightens the OR to an XOR, i.e. the generalization set should be labeled with {complete, disjoint}. A vendor representative confirmed on a call on 2023-10-31 that this was a known issue, which is fixed in a version of CCM later than V19.0 SP4 (which was the version used for import).

It is not clear why this is only asserted in a comment and not made machine readable with a Subproperty Of assertion in the skos:core RDF file.

The labelling in the XMI is assumed to be an error, so VocabularyEntry:mvfEntryStatus is renamed to VocabularyEntry:VocabularyEntryStatus and an enum is defined for its type,

Because Status is a potentially useful attribute for other types of MVFElement a top-level attribute is defined in the profile, which is then subsetted/redefined to implement the various status attribute/property/class definitions in the specifications.

• The classes named Status are represented in the metamodel, but only implemented in the profile as tagged values.

• According to the definition in the MVF specification PDF, status is a "Link to an optional rating established from a predetermined scale and used to evaluate the standing of a term (vocabulary entry) in the context of a given vocabulary". Because different sub-types of MVFElement are likely to require different scales, the abstract attribute is defined as a string literal to allow flexibility. Specific implementations can redefine the property to use enumerations where applicable (in this model applies to VocabularyEntryStatus).

• Multiplicity of the abstract MVFElement:status attribute is unlimited because subtypes may have no status fields or several. Sub-types should restrict this multiplicity in order to ensure that multiple statuses cannot exist for the same aspect of the element.

• The mvfEntryStatus attribute is typed as boolean in the XMI specification, but this is implemented in the profile as a string literal in accordance with the above point.

The MVF specification does not make clear what values mvfEntryStatus should have, so an enum is defined that fits with the original intended purpose of this profile (i.e. vocabulary management for model-based ontology engineering). The enum may require modification if the profile is applied for other purposes.

When CCM transforms OWL ontologies as they are imported from RDF to UML, any RDF properties that the transformer doesn't recognize are rendered as UML associations. This works well for most relations (because a lot of relations in UML models tend to be associations), but it is problematic when the semantics of the property would be better represented with a standard UML relationship other than association. In this model, this applies in particular to relationships that indicate that one element depends on another (e.g. a definition adopted from another vocabulary), which are more naturally represented as UML dependencies. UML associations do not have an attribute that can be used to indicate either general directionality or dependency: the only support for directional attributes is for reading direction (which does not suffice as an assertion of dependency) and navigability (which is a dependency, but only applies to efficiency of runtime access).

 

There is no way for the importer to know the semantics of the imported property automatically (without connecting it to some kind of reasoning engine). This means that the semantics must be applied manually by human review of the model. There are several possible ways to resolve this.

  • Repurpose the navigability property to indicate a directional association
    • This is a fairly common informal practice adopted by many modelers in search of a way to add an arrowhead to an association, but has several drawbacks. The UML 2.5.1 specification states that "Navigability means that instances participating in links at runtime (instances of an Association) can be accessed efficiently from instances at the other ends of the Association". For conceptual modeling, this is not a particular useful property, so within controlled contexts (e.g. a model used only by a single organization) it can be acceptable to redefine the meaning of the navigability arrowhead, provided everyone working on the model is made aware. Because the intended output of this model is a broadly useful UML profile for modeling multiple contexts, this is not an appropriate choice here.
  • Manually refactor the type on the each imported relationship (e.g. change its type from association to dependency)
    • This could cause compatibility problems if the model is used to generate 'round trip' outputs to RDF because information is potentially lost (associations have a different set of attributes than dependencies).
  • Establish newly created "mirror" relationships with the correct type (e.g. dependency) in the metamodel, with traceability links to the property that was imported as an association.
    • This approach is time consuming, increases the maintenance burden, and generates unnecessary duplication.
  • Retain Association as the base type and extend this through inheritance of additional properties through multiple inheritance (e.g. those relationships that are dependencies would have stereotypes «association» and «dependency»).
    • This is a fairly clean solution, but it is not parsimonious because the relationships inherit additional properties that are not strictly necessary. This potentially undermines the benefits of the separation of concerns implicit in the intentional disjointedness of these metaclasses in the UML specification.
  • The cleanest, most parsimonious solution identified, which is used here, is to define custom stereotypes based on standard UML metaclasses in a profile based on the metamodel (see mappingRelation - Top levels).
    • Custom stereotypes ensure that the relationships only have the required properties from the relevant metaclasses. This avoids unnecessary multiple inheritance.

Adopting this final approach means that it is not possible to define relationships based on the custom stereotypes in the metamodel, because this would otherwise create a circular dependency by applying a stereotype in the model that is also defined by the same model. Avoiding this ensures a degree of self-bootstrapping, in that the model can be loaded without needing to preload any profiles to support custom types (except those used from the CCM profile) and can generate the MBOE profile from only standard UML metaclasses.

 

One side effect of the adopted approach is that it is not possible to represent the extensions to skos:mappingRelation directly in the UML metamodel, because CCM converts all the relevant RDF object properties to associations. The disadvantage is that the metamodel does not contain elements representing all the relationships defined in the MBOE profile. Instead, these are declared only as stereotypes on profile diagrams. To assert the mappings from the profile to the metamodel, UML realization relationships (a type of dependency) are shown from top level stereotype elements (which have various metaclasses declared here) to the corresponding imported RDF properties (which are all of type association) in diagram mappingRelation - SKOS to profile mapping. Model-Based Ontology Engineering (MBOE) is the topic of this work. This model provides the UML metamodel and UML profile definition for MBOE.


The purpose of the MBOE profile is to provide vocabulary management for multicontext modelling. It implements most of the MVF metamodel, with the exception of runtime support for dynamic vocabulary switching, combined with SKOS mappingRelation extensions. Broader/narrower map directly to SKOS mappingRelations and convey whether one concept is broader or narrower than the other (e.g. in UML represented by class inheritance and/or parthood relationships). For example, a fleet is a broader concept than a vehicle (i.e. a collection is broader than its member), an engine is a narrower concept than a car (i.e. a part is narrower than the whole in composition hierarchy), and a vehicle is a broader concept than a car (a type is broader than its sub-types).

 

Overlaps is an extension provided by this model that covers cases where some aspects of the compared concepts are broader, but others narrower, or where the things that are compared share common some common characteristics (but not in a hierarchical way). For example, the concept of a bus overlaps with that of a car, because both share the characteristic of conveying loads.
